```{r setup}
#| include: false

library(countdown)
library(mosaic)

knitr::opts_chunk$set(
  fig.width = 8,
  fig.asp = 0.618,
  fig.retina = 3,
  dpi = 300,
  out.width = "80%",
  fig.align = "center"
)

# load packages
library(tidyverse)   # for data wrangling and visualization
library(ggformula)   # for plotting using formulas
library(broom)       # for formatting model output
library(knitr)       # for pretty tables
library(kableExtra)  # also for pretty tables
library(coursekata)  # for resample(), do(), shuffle()
library(plotly)      # for the 3D wobble pictures (loaded last: it masks coursekata's do())

# Coffee truck data: the same pre-generated experiment as AE 17 / AE 18 / HW 08.
# 180 shifts, 15 per Location x TimeOfDay cell, Price fixed at $3.
coffee <- read_csv("https://docs.google.com/spreadsheets/d/e/2PACX-1vREJa-pGZtlZ6daqYK2R1-jHQv5k48uEQ5Lsu4ci_Nyu8IUqGs0zPui8cYVOy9nXJNbd4bm-gLQO0AB/pub?output=csv") |>
  mutate(TimeOfDay = factor(TimeOfDay, levels = c("Morning", "Lunch", "Afternoon")))

# Business vs. City Hall, all three times of day
bc <- coffee |> filter(Location %in% c("Business", "CityHall"))

# sim_xy(): n points where corr(X1, X2) is exactly r, and
# y = 2 + 0*X1 + 1*X2 + noise (so the true X1 slope is 0).
# Same seed => same X1 and same noise, so r is the only thing that changes between pictures.
sim_xy <- function(r, n = 40, sigma = 1.5, beta = c(2, 0, 1), seed = 1) {
  set.seed(seed)
  z1 <- as.numeric(scale(rnorm(n)))
  z2 <- as.numeric(scale(resid(lm(rnorm(n) ~ z1))))
  x2 <- r * z1 + sqrt(1 - r^2) * z2
  tibble(x1 = z1, x2 = x2,
         y = beta[1] + beta[2] * z1 + beta[3] * x2 + rnorm(n, 0, sigma))
}

# wobble_plot(): 3D scatterplot of simulated data with the fitted plane y ~ x1 + x2.
# The "New noise" button redraws the noise in y, refits the plane, and updates the plot,
# all in the browser (the x values and the true plane never change).
wobble_plot <- function(r, sigma = 1.5, beta = c(2, 0, 1), lim = 2.5) {
  d <- sim_xy(r, sigma = sigma, beta = beta)
  b <- coef(lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = d))
  zmat <- function(b) matrix(b[1] + b[2] * rep(c(-lim, lim), times = 2) + b[3] * rep(c(-lim, lim), each = 2),
                             nrow = 2, byrow = TRUE)
  label <- function(b) sprintf("Fitted slopes: b1 = %.2f, b2 = %.2f   (truth: b1 = %g, b2 = %g)",
                               b[2], b[3], beta[2], beta[3])
  plot_ly(height = 450) |>
    add_trace(x = d$x1, y = d$x2, z = d$y, type = "scatter3d", mode = "markers",
              marker = list(size = 3, color = "#C0392B"), showlegend = FALSE) |>
    add_surface(x = c(-lim, lim), y = c(-lim, lim), z = zmat(b), opacity = 0.75,
                colorscale = list(c(0, "#533860"), c(1, "#533860")), showscale = FALSE) |>
    layout(scene = list(xaxis = list(title = "X1", range = c(-lim, lim)),
                        yaxis = list(title = "X2", range = c(-lim, lim)),
                        zaxis = list(title = "Y", range = c(-12, 16)),
                        aspectmode = "cube",
                        camera = list(eye = list(x = 1.7, y = -1.7, z = 0.7))),
           autosize = TRUE,
           margin = list(l = 0, r = 0, t = 30, b = 0),
           annotations = list(list(text = label(b), x = 0.5, y = 1, xref = "paper", yref = "paper",
                                   showarrow = FALSE, font = list(size = 16))),
           updatemenus = list(list(type = "buttons", showactive = FALSE, x = 0, y = 0.9,
                                   buttons = list(list(method = "skip", label = "New noise"))))) |>
    config(displayModeBar = FALSE) |>
    htmlwidgets::onRender("
      function(el, x, d) {
        var n = d.x1.length, L = d.lim;
        function gauss() { var u = 1 - Math.random(), v = Math.random();
                           return Math.sqrt(-2 * Math.log(u)) * Math.cos(2 * Math.PI * v); }
        // least squares for y ~ 1 + x1 + x2 via the normal equations (3 x 3 Gaussian elimination)
        function fit(y) {
          var A = [[0,0,0],[0,0,0],[0,0,0]], c = [0,0,0], i, j, k, row;
          for (i = 0; i < n; i++) {
            row = [1, d.x1[i], d.x2[i]];
            for (j = 0; j < 3; j++) { c[j] += row[j] * y[i];
                                      for (k = 0; k < 3; k++) A[j][k] += row[j] * row[k]; }
          }
          for (j = 0; j < 3; j++) {
            for (i = j + 1; i < 3; i++) { var f = A[i][j] / A[j][j];
              for (k = j; k < 3; k++) A[i][k] -= f * A[j][k]; c[i] -= f * c[j]; }
          }
          var b = [0,0,0];
          for (j = 2; j >= 0; j--) { var s = c[j];
            for (k = j + 1; k < 3; k++) s -= A[j][k] * b[k]; b[j] = s / A[j][j]; }
          return b;
        }
        el.on('plotly_buttonclicked', function() {
          var y = [], i;
          for (i = 0; i < n; i++) y.push(d.beta[0] + d.beta[1] * d.x1[i] + d.beta[2] * d.x2[i] + d.sigma * gauss());
          var b = fit(y), e = [-L, L];
          var z = e.map(function(x2) { return e.map(function(x1) { return b[0] + b[1] * x1 + b[2] * x2; }); });
          Plotly.restyle(el, {z: [y]}, [0]);
          Plotly.restyle(el, {z: [z]}, [1]);
          Plotly.relayout(el, {'annotations[0].text': 'Fitted slopes: b1 = ' + b[1].toFixed(2) +
            ', b2 = ' + b[2].toFixed(2) + '   (truth: b1 = ' + d.beta[1] + ', b2 = ' + d.beta[2] + ')'});
        });
      }", data = list(x1 = d$x1, x2 = d$x2, beta = beta, sigma = sigma, lim = lim))
}

# set default theme and larger font size for ggplot2
ggplot2::theme_set(ggplot2::theme_bw(base_size = 20))
```

# Categorical predictors

## Categorical predictors: tests against a reference level {.smaller}

```{r}
lm(Sales ~ Location, data = coffee) |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3)
```

Each `Location` p-value compares that location with the **reference level** (Business), not with every other location.

```{r}
#| code-line-numbers: "|2"
coffee |>
  mutate(Location = relevel(factor(Location), ref = "Zoo")) |>
  lm(Sales ~ Location, data = _) |>
  tidy() |> kable(digits = 3)
```

::: question
What changed when we switched the reference level to Zoo? What stayed the same?
:::

# Review: t-tests in MLR

## Where we are {.smaller}

```{r}
mlr_fit <- lm(Sales ~ Temperature + Location + TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
mlr_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3)
```

Each row is a $t$-test of $H_0: \beta_j = 0$ **given the other predictors**.

::: question
`Location` has three rows (`LocationCityHall`, `LocationPark`, `LocationZoo`). Each compares one location with the Business District. Is there a single p-value that answers "does `Location` matter at all?"
:::

# A correction: what do we shuffle?

## Correction: shuffle the **response** {.smaller}

Last time I said that, to test one coefficient, we shuffle the **explanatory** variable. **That was wrong.** We shuffle the **response**:

```{r}
#| eval: false
lm(shuffle(Sales) ~ Temperature + TimeOfDay, data = coffee) # correct: shuffle the response
lm(Sales ~ shuffle(Temperature) + TimeOfDay, data = coffee) # wrong: shuffle an explanatory variable
```

. . .

- Shuffling `Sales` breaks the link between the response and **all** of the predictors, but the predictors stay exactly as we observed them, **including how they relate to each other**.
- Shuffling `Temperature` also breaks the relationship between `Temperature` and `TimeOfDay`. The shuffled data sets have predictors that look nothing like ours.

::: question
Why might it matter if the shuffled data sets have predictors that are related differently from the real ones?
:::

## Does it matter? {.smaller}

A simulated data set where `X1` and `X2` are highly correlated ($r = 0.95$), and the true slope of `X1` is **0**:

```{r}
#| echo: false
corr_data <- sim_xy(r = 0.95)
```

```{r shuffle-compare}
#| fig-height: 3.2
corr_fit <- lm(y ~ x1 + x2, data = corr_data)
set.seed(2026)
shuf_y <- mosaic::do(1000) * lm(mosaic::shuffle(y) ~ x1 + x2, data = corr_data)
shuf_x <- mosaic::do(1000) * lm(y ~ mosaic::shuffle(x1) + x2, data = corr_data)

bind_rows(tibble(method = "Shuffle Y (correct)", slope = shuf_y$x1),
          tibble(method = "Shuffle X1 (wrong)", slope = shuf_x[[2]])) |>
  gf_histogram(~ slope | method, bins = 30, fill = "grey80", color = "white") |>
  gf_vline(xintercept = coef(corr_fit)[["x1"]], color = "#533860", linewidth = 1.2) |>
  gf_labs(x = "X1 slope from a shuffled data set", y = "Number of shuffles")
```

::: question
Which null distribution is narrower? What would that do to the p-value? To see why, look at the next two slides.
:::

## Correlated predictors: a wobbly plane {.smaller}

`X1` and `X2` are highly correlated ($r = 0.95$). The truth: `Y` depends on `X2` only (true `X1` slope = 0).

```{r}
#| echo: false
wobble_plot(r = 0.95)
```

::: question
Click **New noise** several times (you can also rotate the plot). What does the plane do? How far does the `X1` slope stray from 0?
:::

## Uncorrelated predictors: a steady plane {.smaller}

Same `X1`, same noise, same truth, but now `X1` and `X2` are uncorrelated ($r = 0$).

```{r}
#| echo: false
wobble_plot(r = 0)
```

::: question
Compare with the last slide. Why does the plane wobble so much less?
:::

## Why this matters for shuffling {.smaller}

- When `X1` and `X2` are correlated, the data can't easily separate their effects: many different planes fit almost equally well. So $\hat\beta_1$ varies a lot from sample to sample, and its **standard error is large**.
- Shuffling `X1` would make it uncorrelated with `X2`, turning the wobbly picture into the steady one. The null distribution would be **too narrow** and the p-values **too small**.
- Shuffling `Y` keeps the correlation between the predictors, so the null distribution reflects the wobble we really have.

**Shuffle the response.**

# Testing Batches Of Coefficients

## Nested models {.smaller}

A $t$-test checks **one** coefficient. To test several coefficients at once (like all the `Location` dummies), we compare two models.

Model A is **nested** in Model B if B contains every predictor/coefficient in A, plus more. Setting the extra coefficients in B to 0 gives you A.

| This model | is nested in this model | The extra terms |
|:---|:---|:---|
| `Sales ~ Temperature + TimeOfDay` | `Sales ~ Temperature + Location + TimeOfDay` | 3 `Location` dummies |
| `Sales ~ Location + TimeOfDay` | `Sales ~ Location * TimeOfDay` | the interaction terms |
| `Sales ~ Temperature` | `Sales ~ Location` | none: **not nested** |

When comparing models, we call the smaller model the **reduced model** and the larger model the **full model**.

. . .

::: question
- Why is `Sales ~ Temperature` not nested in `Sales ~ Location`? 
- Name a model that `Sales ~ Temperature` **is** nested in.
:::

## The $F$-test {.smaller}

- A full model will always result in a higher $R^2$ and a lower $SSE$
- Question: Is the improvement to be worth the extra terms?

. . .

We measure fit with the **sum of squared errors**, $SSE = \sum (y_i - \hat y_i)^2$:

$$
F = \frac{(SSE_{\text{reduced}} - SSE_{\text{full}}) \,/\, (\text{number of extra coefficients})}{SSE_{\text{full}} \,/\, df_{\text{full}}}
$$

- **Numerator:** the improvement in fit **per extra coefficient**.
- **Denominator:** the leftover noise per residual degree of freedom, i.e. $\hat\sigma_\epsilon^2$ of the full model.
- If the extra terms do nothing, $F$ is near 1. A large $F$ means the full model fits much better than we would expect from noise.

. . .

$H_0$: all the extra coefficients are 0 (the reduced model is enough). 

$H_A$: at least one is not 0. 

The p-value comes from an $F$ distribution with (extra coefficients, $df_{\text{full}}$) degrees of freedom.

## Using `anova()` {.smaller}

Give `anova()` the **reduced model first**, then the **full model**.

```{r}
reduced <- lm(Sales ~ Temperature + TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
full <- lm(Sales ~ Temperature + Location + TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
anova(reduced, full) |> tidy() |> kable()
```

| Column | Meaning |
|:---|:---|
| `df.residual`/`Res.Df` | residual degrees of freedom of each model |
| `RSS` | the sum of squared errors ($SSE$) of each model. R labels it "residual sum of squares" |
| `df` | number of extra coefficients in the full model |
| `Sum of Sq` | $SSE_{\text{reduced}} - SSE_{\text{full}}$ |
| `statistics` and `p.value`/`F` and `Pr(>F)` | the test statistic and its p-value |

. . .

::: question
How many extra coefficients does `full` have? Check that `Sum of Sq` equals the difference in the two `RSS` values.
:::

## One test for a whole variable {.smaller}

Does `Location` matter **at all**, after accounting for `Temperature` and `TimeOfDay`? That is the `anova(reduced, full)` comparison we just ran.

- $H_0$: all `Location` coefficients are 0.
- A small p-value says at least one location differs, but not which. For that, look at the individual $t$-tests (the reference-level comparisons).

::: question
What do you conclude about `Location`? What would you conclude if the p-value were 0.6?
:::

## F-Test = T-Test for One Coefficient {.smaller}

:::: columns
::: column
```{r}
full_model <- lm(Sales ~ Temperature + TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
full_model |> tidy() |> kable()
```
:::
::: column
```{r}
reduced_model <- lm(Sales~ TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
anova(reduced_model, full_model) |> tidy() |> kable()
```
:::
::::

Exactly the same!

## Do we need the interaction? {.smaller}

```{r}
lm(Sales ~ Location * Temperature, data = bc) |> tidy() |> kable() # bc is just the business and city hall data
```

- The interaction p-value tests: "**does the effect of one variable depend on the other?**"
- Main-effect p-values become hard to interpret and can safely be ignored... Once interaction is important, both variables that are interacting must also be important.
- Keep both main effects in the model whenever you keep their interaction.

::: question
Interpret this p-value in context. What would you tell Jo?
:::

## P-values in the interaction model {.smaller}

```{r}
int_fit <- lm(Sales ~ Location * TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
int_fit |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3)
```

::: question
This case has MULTIPLE interactions terms for the same two variables... How can we test them all at once?
:::

. . .

```{r}
add_fit <- lm(Sales ~ Location + TimeOfDay, data = coffee)
anova(add_fit, int_fit) |> tidy() |> kable()
```


## "Not significant" is not "no effect" {.smaller}

```{r}
set.seed(2026)
small <- bc |> filter(TimeOfDay == "Lunch") |> group_by(Location) |> slice_sample(n = 4) |> ungroup()
lm(Sales ~ Location, data = small) |> tidy() |> kable(digits = 3)
```

The full Lunch data showed a difference of about 18 cups. With 4 days per location, the p-value is large.

::: question
Does a large p-value mean City Hall and the Business District sell the same amount? What went wrong? (Hint: Lessons 14-16.)
:::

## Recap {.smaller}

- Model A is **nested** in Model B if B has every term in A plus more.
- The $F$-test compares the **sum of squared errors** of a reduced and a full model: is the improvement more than noise?
- Use `anova(reduced, full)` to test a whole variable, or an interaction, at once.
- With an interaction, main-effect p-values are conditional, and the interaction p-value asks whether the effect **depends on** the other variable.
- Many tests mean many chances for false positives: name your primary hypothesis in advance.
- A large p-value with a small sample is not evidence of no effect.

## Coming next {.smaller}

A p-value only tells us whether a coefficient could be 0. It does not tell us **how big** the effect is, or how precisely we have estimated it.

::: question
Jo's data say City Hall sells about 18 more cups at Lunch. How sure are we about that number?
:::

Next time: **confidence intervals**.
